analysis.one_liner: Requires companies with 500+ workers to publicly report workplace deaths, injuries, and illnesses.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a House floor vote; after introduction it was referred to the Education and Labor Committee and a subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Labor Department to write rules requiring large employers — companies with at least 500 employees across more than one worksite — to keep accurate records of work-related deaths, injuries, and illnesses at each site and to file certified annual reports. Those reports, along with each site's inspection history and violations, would be posted on the Department of Labor's public website. Companies that failed to report could be cited under the Occupational Safety and Health Act, even in states that run their own workplace-safety programs.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at large companies would gain a public, site-by-site record of injuries, illnesses, and fatalities at their employer — including inspection results and citations — letting them see safety risks before they are harmed, letting unions and community groups target the most dangerous worksites, and letting regulators spot chronic underreporting. The public would also gain, since all reports would be posted on the Labor Department website.

how_it_helps.text: Requires large employers to keep accurate records of work-related deaths, injuries, and illnesses at each establishment and to file certified annual reports with the Secretary of Labor.
Requires each report to include compliance data such as inspection numbers and dates and the total number of violations and citations issued following inspections.
Requires the Labor Department to post all such reports on its public website within six months of each reporting deadline.

Requires employers to identify each establishment and flag any site that has been acquired, sold, or transferred, limiting the ability to lose track of a site's safety history through corporate restructuring.
Lets the Labor Department cite any covered employer for violating the reporting requirements, including employers in states with approved state workplace-safety plans.

analysis.who_pays: Large employers — companies with 500 or more employees at multiple sites — would bear the cost of maintaining accurate site-level records and preparing certified annual reports, plus the public exposure of their injury and inspection records, which could bring reputational damage, regulatory scrutiny, or pressure to fix hazards. Small employers with fewer than 10 employees per site and the construction industry are excluded.

drawbacks.text: Covered employers would face new recordkeeping and reporting costs and certified-reporting liability, which businesses generally argued was duplicative of existing OSHA recordkeeping obligations (the bill builds on existing 29 CFR 1904 recordkeeping definitions rather than creating an entirely new system).

The bill targets only companies with at least 500 employees across multiple sites, so most worksites — including all construction sites and any establishment with fewer than 10 employees — fall outside its reporting requirements, leaving many of the most dangerous industries uncovered.

Public posting of site-level injury data could invite misreading of raw numbers, since injury rates vary by industry and reporting practices, potentially penalizing employers that report honestly relative to those that underreport.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is cheap and real: injury and fatality data already largely exists under OSHA rules, and the bill mainly requires large employers to certify it site-by-site and make it public. The compliance cost is modest and falls on a small number of very large companies. The design has real gaps — construction and small sites are excluded — but the public benefit of transparent, site-level safety data outweighs the burden on large employers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Education and Labor Committee, which passed it down to its Workforce Protections subcommittee in June 2009; no further action was taken before the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Phil Hare introduced the Corporate Injury, Illness, and Fatality Reporting Act of 2009 on April 27, 2009, with 13 original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the day it was introduced.
On June 4, 2009, it was referred to the committee's Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, and the record shows no markup, hearing, or floor action afterward.
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and the bill never received a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large multi-site employers are better off: they never had to publish certified, site-by-site injury and inspection records or face citations for reporting failures, and no additional recordkeeping or public exposure was imposed. Workers at those companies did not get the public safety data the bill promised.

for.name: Phil Hare
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: George Miller
for.role: U.S. Representative, CA-7; original cosponsor and chair of the Education and Labor Committee
for.what_they_did: Was an original cosponsor of the bill; as committee chair he controlled whether it received a markup or floor scheduling, and the record shows none occurred.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Took no further action after referring the bill to its Workforce Protections subcommittee on June 4, 2009; the bill died there without a markup or a vote.

against.name: Subcommittee on Workforce Protections
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 4, 2009 and never reported the bill back to the full committee.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 17 cosponsors were House Democrats, and no Republican cosponsored; because the bill never reached the floor, no roll-call vote shows how the parties would have split.

industries.note: The bill would have required these companies to certify and publicly disclose site-by-site injury, illness, and fatality counts along with their OSHA inspection and citation histories, exposing safety problems to workers, regulators, and the public. Workers' interest in seeing that data runs directly against employers' interest in keeping it private.

Construction is explicitly excluded from the bill's definitions, so construction employers would have avoided the new reporting duties — a gain for the industry, but one that left workers in one of the most dangerous industries without the disclosure the bill offered elsewhere.
